Restrict the transition to pending and surface a typed error when no row was updated.

content: notif_sync_memory rewrites the JSON payload with only `{"ids": remaining}`, discarding every other key that may have been stored. If the payload ever carries additional metadata (e.g. session id, timestamps, summaries), this UPDATE will silently delete that information. Preserve the original payload by merging `remaining` into the existing object instead of replacing it.

`notif_resolve_artifact` loads every pending artifact notification, parses each payload in Rust, and only then filters by `taskId`. With many pending rows this is O(N) memory + JSON parsing per call. Use SQLite's `json_extract` (or a dedicated indexed column) so the filter runs in SQL, and wrap the updates in a transaction so a failure leaves the table consistent.

`notif_sync_memory` issues one `SELECT COUNT(*)` per id (N+1 queries) and `unwrap_or(false)` swallows any DB error as "not present". If a transient error occurs or the payload contains non‑integer ids, `remaining` can become empty and the notification will be prematurely resolved. Fetch the pending ids in a single query, build a `HashSet`, and treat unknown/parse‑error IDs as fatal for that notification rather than silently discarding them.

`profile_remove_avatar` deletes whatever path `profile_dir(&app).join(f)` resolves to without re‑validating `f` via `avatar_filename_only`. A hand‑edited / imported / corrupt `profile.json` can put values such as `"../../wmessage.db"`, `"/etc/passwd"`, `"a\\b.png"` or even an absolute path into `avatar`; after the function successfully clears the JSON reference (which only requires the read‑modify‑write lock) the next line will unlink that arbitrary file with the privileges of the Tauri process. Because the field is also accepted from the IPC layer, this is reachable from any compromised renderer as well. Validate the stored name through `avatar_filename_only` (rejecting `None`) and, on rejection, audit the event instead of deleting. Optionally also verify the resolved path is a child of `profile_dir` (canonicalize both) before `remove_file`.

`profile_set_avatar` deletes *all* prior avatars for this `kind` **before** the new avatar is committed. If `std::fs::copy`, `save_data`, or the final `rename` later fails, `profile.json` is left pointing at the old filename (or at the new filename when the save succeeded but the rename did not) while the old file is already gone — the user's previous avatar is silently lost with no rollback path. Defer deletion of the previously stored avatar (and any other‑extension siblings) until **after** `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)` succeeds; only then look up the prior `entry.avatar` recorded before the overwrite and remove it. The cleanup loop should keep `dest` (or the old extension's file) untouched until the new file is on disk.

The new avatar is committed in the order `save_data(&profile.json)` → `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)`. Because `profile.json` is updated *before* the on‑disk file is in place, a failure of `rename` (cross‑device move, AV/EBUSY, Windows sharing violation, quota, etc.) leaves `profile.json` pointing at a filename that does not exist (or, after the old file was removed by the earlier cleanup loop, pointing at a file that was never created). The function then returns `Err`, but the persisted state is already inconsistent — the next `profile_get` will return `avatar_data_url=None`. Reverse the ordering: perform `rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)` first while the old entry is still in the JSON, then call `save_data`. If `save_data` fails after the rename, `cleanup_set_avatar_failure` can be extended to revert the rename using `rename(&dest, &dest_tmp)` (or, on platforms where rename‑over‑existing isn’t atomic, remove the new file).

`ensure_person_id` has a classic RMW race: both `pid` (generated before the lock) and `data.person_id` (read inside the lock) are used independently. When two first‑run callers race, each persists *its own* `pid` to `profile.json` via the double‑check (only the second sees the first's write, the first has already finished), and then both still call `people_upsert_entry(&pid, …, is_self=true)` using their *local* `pid`. Result: two self rows in `people` with different ids while only one of them ends up in `profile.json`; every subsequent export uses the surviving id and the orphan self row leaks. On `save_data` failure the function still upserts `pid` and returns it as if persisted, breaking the documented "固化 idempotent" contract and producing a fresh self row on the next call. Fix: under the lock load `profile.json`, compute the canonical pid (`existing or newly generated`), write it, capture it from the locked `data`, and use that canonical value for the `people_upsert_entry` and the return tuple; also propagate the `save_data` error (change the signature to `CommandResult`) so the caller does not get a non‑persistent pid.

`entry_view` blindly `metadata()`/`read()`s whatever file sits at `profile_dir(app).join(f)`. The filename validation only rejects literal `/`, `\` and `..`; it does **not** inspect the file itself. If an attacker (or a hostile dropper in a portable install on a shared drive) can plant a symlink at `profile/avatar-user.png` pointing at e.g. `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, the next `profile_get` will read that file, base64‑encode it, and emit it to every window via the `profile-changed` IPC event. Use `std::fs::symlink_metadata` and reject (audit + `None`) when the entry's `file_type().is_symlink()` is true, or open with `OpenOptions::new().read(true).custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW)` on platforms that support it.

Prompt instructs `run_python` for bulk cross-file edits and data processing, but the underlying tool (`SCHEMA_RUN_PYTHON`, `run_python_ungated` in `py/runtime.rs`) explicitly provides "无文件系统隔离" — only CPU/memory/time limits are enforced, no chroot/path restriction, so arbitrary Python can read/write anywhere on the user's filesystem, spawn subprocesses, and access the network. The "安全红线" at the end ("绝不执行系统命令、修改系统设置、访问系统目录"; write-tool whitelist "白名单外弹确认") is purely prompt-level and is actively defeated by rule 12 ("用户要写代码/跑数据处理时用 run_python") and rule 19 ("同一处改动散布多个文件或多处重复出现时，用 run_python 批量替换比逐个 edit_file 更高效可靠"). Either tighten the prompt to forbid run_python from touching whitelisted paths / launching subprocesses (relying on prompt adherence is fragile), or back the tool with a real sandbox (chroot, macOS sandbox-exec, Windows Job Object + restricted token, container) so the security red lines become enforced invariants instead of advisory text.

content: Rule 19 actively encourages `run_python` as the preferred bulk-edit path ("用 run_python 批量替换比逐个 edit_file 更高效可靠"), but combined with the lack of filesystem isolation in run_python (see high-severity finding above) this turns the per-call write whitelist into advisory text: the model can iterate the whole filesystem in a single tool call. Recommend rewriting the recommendation to either (a) keep edit_file/write_file as the only sanctioned write path and document run_python's scope as read-only within allowedDirs, or (b) require the same whitelist confirmation flow that edit_file/write_file enforce before any run_python write.

content: VECTOR_CACHE is held across the synchronous `embed_text` call, so a single slow ONNX inference serializes every concurrent caller — including pure cache hits from unrelated commands — for the full inference latency. The inline comment justifies the trade-off, but `tag_similar_pairs` is not the only path that touches this global; any future reader/writer of `VECTOR_CACHE` will block. Drop the lock before the blocking call and re-acquire it just for the insert; the brief race window on a cache miss is acceptable for this workload and can be tightened later with a single-flight guard (e.g. `DashMap` entry API) if duplicate ONNX calls actually show up in profiling.

Guard's ownership check is only `subagent_id` equality, so an ABA scenario — same `session_id` + same `subagent_id` reused by a retry/resume — causes the old guard's Drop to delete the newer runner's registration. This silently disables the recursion gate (`is_subagent_session` returns false) for the live subagent, allowing it to spawn further subagents. The ownership identity should be unique (e.g. an `Arc<()>` weak token, generation counter, or guard-issued nonce) not just a string field that is expected to repeat.

`register_subagent_session` blindly overwrites an existing entry, replacing the `Arc<AtomicUsize>` budget counter. A duplicate registration (retry/reuse of the same session_id, or a buggy double-spawn) resets `used_tool_calls` to whatever the new caller supplies — a second runner can effectively nullify `max_tool_calls` enforcement. Callers that already hold a clone of the old context can still increment the *detached* old counter, bypassing any future re-check. Either reject duplicate keys, or require the new context to carry the *same* `Arc<AtomicUsize>` (carry-and-check) so the counter is preserved across retries.

The task-execution-flow registry has no RAII guard, no ownership check, and no idempotency token. A panic between `register_exec_session` and `unregister_exec_session` permanently leaks the entry (making `is_task_execution_flow` always true). Conversely, session-ID reuse causes the new registration to be silently overwritten, and a late `unregister_exec_session` from the previous (stale) runner removes the new entry — misclassifying a live task execution as a plain conversation. Both `register_exec_session` and `unregister_exec_session` should be wrapped in a guard analogous to `SubagentSessionGuard`, or at minimum check that the current entry's origin matches the one the caller originally registered.

Re-including `tests/mock_llm.rs` via `include!` re-registers every `#[tokio::test]` defined there inside the bot_test_connection binary, so mock_llm's own tests will run twice across the suite (and any shared mutable state across runs could interact). Prefer placing the shared mock under `tests/common/` (a non-test module) and importing from both test binaries, or guard the duplicated tests with `#[cfg(...)]` so they only register in one binary.

Empty LLM result is not idempotent. The pre-read guard only skips when `tags` is already Some(non-empty), and an empty parse result is returned as Ok(Some(vec![])) without persisting any attempt marker. Subsequent invocations that find `tags` still empty will re-enter the full LLM path, contradicting the module-level claim that the guard chain is idempotent. Consider persisting an explicit "attempted, no tags" state (e.g. a separate column or a sentinel tag) or returning a distinct Ok(None) variant so repeated fire-and-forget calls do not re-invoke the model.</content>

eval_extract_sample 写真实用户内容（mem_items.content 等 PII）到 fixtures/memory_extract_sample.jsonl，使用 std::fs::write 继承进程 umask（通常 0644，可被本机其他用户读取），且没有任何清理/老化机制——重复运行会无限累积明文 PII。建议用 OpenOptions::create + libc::chmod（或用 std::os::unix::fs::OpenOptionsExt::mode(0o600)）写入，并在文档注释里明确「标注完请手动 rm」。注释里说「已进 .gitignore 不入库」是软保证，代码自身并未校验 .gitignore 包含该路径，存在误提交风险。

`end_trace` collapses every non-Ok path into `TRACE_STATUS_FAILED` and represents user-/system-initiated stops as `TRACE_STATUS_DONE` because `run_model_loop` returns `Ok` on stop (`bot_model_loop.rs:1267-1270, 1371-1373`) and `run_task_in_chat_with` then calls `end_trace(.., outcome.is_ok(), ..)` (`bot_chat.rs:1863-1870`). The schema defines `TRACE_STATUS_STOPPED` and `TRACE_STATUS_TIMEOUT` (`db/trace.rs:30, 1477`) but they are never produced here, so trace analytics mis-classify cancelled runs as successful. The signature needs an explicit outcome (or status + stop flag) so stopped/timeout paths can be persisted accurately.

`end_trace` removes the `session_id -> trace_id` registry entry and then runs `trace_finish` without waiting for the background writer to drain queued spans/file_changes for this trace. `trace_finish` derives `files_changed` from `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM file_changes WHERE trace_id=?` (`db/trace.rs:286`); if the writer is still holding rows for this trace, the count is permanently under-reported. After commit, late inserts become orphans (no FK). Either drain the channel first (and wait for the writer to ack), or move the registry removal until after `trace_finish` succeeds.

`begin_trace` and `end_trace` run `trace_start` / `trace_finish` on a fresh `Connection` inside `spawn_blocking`, but the module doc explicitly states "与主写者共用 `DB_WRITE_LOCK` 纪律" and the writer carefully takes `crate::db::lock_db_write()` around every batch. Lifecycle writes therefore run concurrently with the writer and any other DB writer, opening the door to `SQLITE_BUSY`, lost updates, and the count race described in the previous finding. Wrap each lifecycle write in the same `lock_db_write()` guard.

The `writer` task is `spawn`ed on the async runtime but performs synchronous `rusqlite` work and holds `crate::db::lock_db_write()` (a `std::sync::Mutex`) across each batch. Under contention or slow disk this blocks an async worker thread and serialises every DB writer on the critical section. Drain the batch into a `Vec` on the async runtime, then perform the actual insert via `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking` so the blocking work does not stall the runtime (and the lock is held off the async task).

Global `intent_router` state is mutated by `rebuild_routes` BEFORE `RoutesResetGuard` is constructed. If the call to `intent_rules_from_dirs` (or anything between the two lines) panics, the global route table is left populated with fixture routes and leaks into subsequent tests in the same `cargo test` binary process — the guard's `Drop` only protects the happy path from the let-binding onward. Bind the guard first so its drop covers the rebuild itself.

The module-wide `#![allow(clippy::await_holding_lock)]` is too broad: only the four `scheduler_e2e_*` tests need it, yet it silently permits any future test in this file to hold a sync Mutex across `.await` without warning. Combined with `make_persist` returning `impl Fn(...) + '_` (borrowing `&conn` across the `.await` inside `run_skill_scheduler_core`), the resulting future is not `'static`; if the scheduler ever spawns the persist closure into a background task the build will fail at the scheduler's spawn site rather than where the lifetime was introduced. Narrow the allow to the four scheduler tests, or move to `tokio::sync::Mutex` and a `'static` executor/persist that owns an `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`.
existing_code: #![allow(clippy::await_holding_lock)]

content: Cross-test config race: `write_config_with_memory_control` uses non-atomic `std::fs::write` on the global `wmessage_lib::bot::config_path(handle)` and `clean_gate_leftovers` then unconditionally removes it. Parallel integration tests in the same process (or any other binary touching the same data dir) can read a half-written JSON, observe a momentarily empty/missing config, or have the file yanked while another test is mid-read. The whole test file also runs under nextest with cross-process shared state for `target/debug/deps/...`, so a single shared config file is a guaranteed race surface. At minimum: write via tempfile + atomic rename, and back up / restore the original contents around the test instead of `remove_file`. Best: move this test to a per-test data dir (e.g. a temp dir passed via `MockRuntime` config) so it cannot collide with any other test.

Cleanup violates the project's DB lock contract. `t1_cleanup` (and the analogous `clean_gate_leftovers`) issue direct `conn.execute("DELETE …")` calls against the shared `target/debug/deps/wmessage.db` without holding `wmessage_lib::db::lock_db_write()`, even though every production write path (`db::upsert_tasks`, `db::upsert_scheduled_job`, `db::workflow_save_locked`) is required to take that guard (C3-1). On a busy run this surfaces as `SQLITE_BUSY` or, worse, silently leaving the shared rows behind because failures are swallowed via `eprintln!`. Two consequences: (1) flake / false-positive assertions in `t1_db_roundtrip_new_columns_and_rmw_edit` and `memory_gate_scenarios_injection_and_auto_write`; (2) cross-test contamination when nextest runs binaries concurrently and deletes mutate rows other tests rely on. Also note the delete order: `DELETE FROM scheduled_jobs` runs before `DELETE FROM scheduled_job_runs`, which will hit a FK violation if the schema defines one — currently swallowed by `eprintln!`. Wrap each delete in `lock_db_write()` and either `.expect(...)` or propagate the error, and delete runs before jobs.

JSON string escaping is incomplete: only `\` and `"` are escaped via two `replace` calls, but newlines (`
`/``), tabs (`	`), backspace, form feed, and other C0 control characters are passed through verbatim into `data: {...}` SSE events and `application/json` bodies. A test that pushes content with a newline (e.g., an assistant message that embeds a quoted multiline block, or a tool argument like `{"code":"
print(1)
"}`) will produce multi-line JSON inside a single `data:` line. SSE parsers and downstream `serde_json::from_str` will then fail on these mock responses in unpredictable ways, hiding real regressions behind mock-side corruption. Replace the two `replace` calls with a real JSON escaper (e.g. iterate bytes and emit `\u00XX` for control chars) or — better — build the payload via `serde_json::json!({...}).to_string()` so escaping is handled correctly. The same fix applies to `sse_text_reply`, `sse_tool_call_reply`, `sse_stream_error_reply`, `anthropic_sse_text_reply`, `anthropic_sse_tool_call_reply`, `anthropic_sse_error_reply`, `anthropic_sse_text_then_tool_call_reply`, the `AnthropicJsonReply` body, and the `OpenAiJsonReply` body — every builder that interpolates a user-controlled string into a JSON literal.

Confirm there is a tracked process to monitor tiny_http advisories, refresh the vendor source when upstream ships a fix, and that the two-file patch scope described in the comment is still accurate; long-term divergence is a real supply-chain risk. Prefer upstreaming the per-connection read timeout or moving it into a thin in-tree wrapper crate so the dep graph stays on the canonical release.

content: This committed setting makes `sccache` a hard prerequisite for every Rust compilation, including the repository's normal `cargo check` pre-commit path. Cargo does not fall back when an executable named `sccache` is absent from `PATH`; it aborts before invoking `rustc`. No project setup script or contributor/CI documentation installs it, so a fresh clone on an otherwise valid Rust toolchain cannot build. Keep this performance optimization out of the shared project config and enable it per developer/CI environment (for example, with `CARGO_BUILD_RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache`), or provision `sccache` in every supported build environment.

content: Implicit `any` on `assetsInlineLimit` predicate: the `(filePath) =>` parameter has no type annotation, so under a strict tsconfig it falls back to `any` (or fails to compile). Per project rules `any` must be avoided — type the parameter explicitly (e.g. `(filePath: string) => boolean | undefined`).

Critical: `__dirname` is undefined in ESM. The project's `package.json` sets `"type": "module"`, so this `.ts` config is loaded as an ES module where `__dirname` does not exist — vitest will throw `ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined` on startup (e.g. `npm test`). Replace with `import.meta.url`-based resolution: `import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url"; const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));` (or just `path.resolve("./src")` works since vitest's cwd is the config dir, but the ESM-safe pattern is preferable).

Path resolution is fragile: `$(dirname "$0")/../scripts/test-all.sh` assumes the hook lives in a directory that is exactly one level below the repo root. If git is configured with a different `core.hooksPath` (e.g., `.githooks/workhorse`), or if the hooks directory is symlinked, `..` will not land on the repo root and `exec` will fail with a cryptic "No such file or directory". Recommend resolving `$0` through symlinks and locating the repo root explicitly: `exec "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/scripts/test-all.sh"`.
suggestion_code: exec "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/scripts/test-all.sh"
existing_code: exec "$(dirname "$0")/../scripts/test-all.sh"

content: This target is derived from the hook's invocation path, not from the repository root that was just selected. That can execute the wrong worktree: with linked worktrees, a shared absolute `core.hooksPath` may point at worktree A while the hook is running for worktree B; the wrapper then launches A's `test-fast.sh`, which runs its checks against A and can incorrectly pass a commit made in B. A relative `$0` is also reinterpreted after the `cd`. Capture the root before changing directories and derive the target from that root (or resolve the hook path before changing directories).
suggestion_code:
if ! repo_root="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"; then
    echo "[pre-commit] 无法定位 repo root" >&2
    exit 1
fi
cd -- "$repo_root" || { echo "[pre-commit] 无法进入 repo root: $repo_root" >&2; exit 1; }
_test_fast="$repo_root/scripts/test-fast.sh"
existing_code: _test_fast="$(dirname "$0")/../scripts/test-fast.sh"
